extracted.intended_audience: aspiring playwrights, screenwriters, and creative writers interested in dramatic craft
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and evaluative criteria for writing dramatic works (plays, screenplays, and fiction) focusing on premise, character, conflict, structure, and pacing. Extracted from reader commentary on Lajos Egri's The Art of Dramatic Writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character backstory / biography
rubrics_metrics.description: The writer must know characters very well (more than what is revealed to the audience).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use detailed biographies as hidden material — the audience sees only a fraction (iceberg metaphor). Failing to do this will show as inaccuracies or shallow characterization. Even if you develop characters while writing, the hidden background must exist to make on-page behavior authentic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clear, unified premise
rubrics_metrics.description: The story must have a clear premise that the work is trying to demonstrate or argue; the premise must be known clearly at some stage of writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Premise need not be fixed at the outset but must be clarified by some stage; all pieces of the story must fit this premise. Anti-patterns: a work that 'tries to prove too many points at once' or where the second half 'drags' because the pieces don't cohere. Scoring note: cohesion of events and theme with stated/implicit premise is critical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Premise-character alignment
rubrics_metrics.description: The premise has to match your character and story — events must be chosen based on character to convincingly argue the premise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: In A Doll's House, Nora's character must align with the resolution for it to work; if the character were different the resolution would fail. Choose situations appropriate to the main character so the plot naturally proves the premise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character-driven action and opposing motivations
rubrics_metrics.description: Each character must have a driving reason to be on stage, and characters' reasons should be diametrically opposed so that not everyone can get what they want.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characters should actively pursue goals (be 'desperate enough to be interesting') rather than passively being acted upon. Conflict should be zero-sum in dramatic terms: one character's gain often necessitates another's loss. Anti-patterns include passive characters or motivations that don't generate meaningful opposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate type and use of conflict
rubrics_metrics.description: Select the kind of conflict suitable for the story; different types of conflict exist and should be used intentionally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Egri discusses different types of conflict and when to use each. Choose the conflict type that best serves the premise and character dynamics rather than defaulting to generic conflict. Examples and play analyses are recommended to learn effective deployment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Planning, architecture, and pacing
rubrics_metrics.description: Good dramatic writing requires planning and architectural design because pacing is crucial, especially in plays and screenplays.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Think in terms of set-up, turning points, climax, and resolution, and construct the story so momentum and timing work for performance. Anti-patterns: insufficient planning leading to pacing problems or uneven middle sections. Scoring guidance: assess how well structure supports pacing and dramatic tension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effective turning points and resolutions
rubrics_metrics.description: Turning points and the resolution must arise from character and premise and must be the right kinds of moments for the story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask 'what makes a good turning point' and 'what makes a good resolution' — they should follow logically from character choices and the premise. Bad turning points feel unearned or misaligned with character and theme.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implied beginnings and necessary implications
rubrics_metrics.description: Every story must have a beginning (and constituent parts), even if the beginning isn't shown on the page; elements not shown must be implied by what is shown.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure that off-page backstory and prior events are properly implied in on-page action and dialogue so the audience can infer the necessary foundations. Anti-patterns: missing implications that leave plot or character motives unexplained.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus: avoid proving too many points
rubrics_metrics.description: A strong dramatic work focuses on a central idea or argument rather than attempting to prove multiple disparate points.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer focused and revealing writing over unfocused and confusing narratives. Works that attempt to make too many arguments dilute thematic power and confuse pacing and character motivation.
